repos.description: On-device LoRA fine-tuning for small language models on Apple silicon and Jetson devices
repos.readme_text:
# tinytune

Fine-tune small language models directly on edge hardware. No cloud round-trip, no data leaving the device.

## Why

Existing fine-tuning stacks assume you have a datacenter GPU. tinytune targets the opposite end: a single Jetson Orin, a Raspberry Pi 5 with 16GB, or an M-series laptop with unified memory.

It does three things:

1. Profile your model and pick a quantization scheme (int4 / int8 / mixed) that fits your memory budget.
2. Build a LoRA adapter with a memory-aware rank selection instead of a fixed rank.
3. Export a GGUF bundle that llama.cpp can load directly.

## Quick start

```bash
pip install tinytune
tinytune profile --model Qwen2.5-0.5B --device jetson-orin
tinytune train --data mydata.jsonl --target-memory 3gb
tinytune export --format gguf
```

## Measured results

| Device | Model | Peak RAM | Tokens/s after | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Jetson Orin Nano 8GB | Qwen2.5-0.5B | 2.4 GB | 41 |
| Raspberry Pi 5 16GB | Qwen2.5-0.5B | 2.1 GB | 12 |
| M2 Air 16GB | Llama-3.2-1B | 3.8 GB | 58 |

## Limitations

- Only LoRA and QLoRA, no full fine-tuning.
- Training above 1B parameters is not supported yet.
- Windows support is experimental.

## License

MIT

repos.description: MCP gateway with per-tool rate limiting, audit logging and replay for production agent deployments
repos.readme_text:
# mcp-gateway

A production gateway that sits between your agent and its MCP servers.

Most teams wire MCP servers directly into the agent process. That works until you need to know which tool call burned your budget, or you want to replay a failed run, or one misbehaving tool takes down the whole session.

## What it does

- **Per-tool rate limits and quotas.** Configure `filesystem.read` at 100 calls/min while leaving `search` unlimited.
- **Structured audit log.** Every tool call, arguments, latency, and result size lands in a JSONL stream you can query.
- **Replay.** Re-run a recorded session against a fixed set of tool responses to reproduce agent bugs deterministically.
- **Circuit breaking.** A tool that fails repeatedly gets quarantined instead of poisoning the context.

## Config

```yaml
tools:
  filesystem.read:
    rate_limit: 100/min
    on_failure: quarantine
  payment.*:
    require_approval: true
```

## Status

v0.1, used internally for a few weeks. The replay format is not frozen yet.

## Roadmap

- OpenTelemetry export
- Per-tenant isolation

repos.description: Deterministic context packing for long-running coding agents
repos.readme_text:
# ctxpack

Context assembly for coding agents that run for hours, not minutes.

The problem: as a session grows, everyone reinvents the same ad-hoc trimming. The agent gets dumber slowly and you cannot tell why.

ctxpack makes context assembly an explicit, inspectable pipeline:

1. **Score** every candidate chunk (file contents, tool output, prior turns) on recency, reference count, and token cost.
2. **Pack** under a token budget with a deterministic tie-break, so the same input always produces the same context.
3. **Explain** why each chunk was kept or dropped.

Determinism matters more than it sounds: it is what makes agent regressions reproducible in CI.

```ts
import { pack } from 'ctxpack'

const { context, report } = pack(chunks, { budget: 120_000 })
console.log(report.dropped) // [{ id, reason: 'budget', score: 0.31 }]
```

## Not trying to be

This is not a vector store and not a RAG framework. It assumes you already retrieved your candidates and now have to fit them into a window.

## License

Apache-2.0

repos.description: Open evaluation harness for RAG pipelines with reproducible scoring and regression detection
repos.readme_text:
# evalharness

Turn RAG evaluation into a regression test instead of a vibes check.

You describe your pipeline once, point evalharness at a golden set, and it produces a diffable report. Run it in CI and you find out that your retrieval change dropped answer faithfulness before your users do.

## Metrics

- retrieval recall@k and MRR
- answer faithfulness via your choice of judge model
- citation precision
- cost and latency per query

## Design notes

Judge models are pluggable and the harness records the judge's exact prompt and version, because a metric you cannot reproduce is not a metric.

```bash
pip install evalharness
evalharness run --config eval.yaml --baseline main.json --out report.html
```

Status: early, the API will move.

repos.description: Inspect and validate GGUF quantization metadata before you run llama.cpp
repos.readme_text:
# gguf-inspect

A small CLI that answers one question: is this GGUF file actually what its filename claims?

Quantization labels in the wild are unreliable. `Q4_K_M` files sometimes contain mixed tensor types, and a mislabeled file produces quietly worse output rather than an error.

```bash
$ gguf-inspect model.Q4_K_M.gguf
file        model.Q4_K_M.gguf
architecture llama
params      7.6B
tensors      291
quant mix   Q4_K 78% | Q6_K 14% | F16 8%
warning     token_embd is Q4_K, most Q4_K_M builds keep it at Q6_K
```

Rust, no dependencies beyond a GGUF reader. Built because I got tired of debugging this by hand.

repos.description: Observability proxy for LLM agent traffic that records every tool call for deterministic replay
repos.readme_text:
# agent-proxy

A local proxy that sits in front of your model API and records the full agent trajectory: prompts, tool calls, tool results, timings, token counts.

Point your OpenAI-compatible client at `http://localhost:8787` and everything gets recorded to `.agent-runs/`.

## Why not just use an existing tracer

Most tracing tools focus on the model calls. Agent failures usually live in the loop: a tool returned something subtly wrong, the agent retried, context filled up, quality collapsed. agent-proxy records the loop, not just the spans.

```bash
npx agent-proxy --upstream https://api.openai.com/v1
```

## Replay

```bash
npx agent-proxy replay .agent-runs/2026-03-11T09:22.json --until step=14
```

Early prototype. Storage format may change.

repos.description: Embedded vector index for SQLite with SIMD distance kernels
repos.readme_text:
# vectorlite

A SQLite extension that adds a vector index. Single file, no server, no separate process.

```sql
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE docs USING vectorlite(embedding, dim=768);
SELECT title FROM docs WHERE embedding MATCH ? ORDER BY distance LIMIT 10;
```

## Numbers

1M x 768 float32 vectors, 8 threads, on an M2:

| Index | Build | Recall@10 | p50 query |
|---|---|---|---|
| HNSW | 214s | 0.97 | 1.8ms |
| IVF-PQ | 71s | 0.89 | 0.9ms |

## Why

If your dataset is under a few million vectors, running a separate vector database in a container is a lot of operational overhead for something that could live in the file you already ship.

## Status

Alpha. HNSW is stable, IVF-PQ is experimental.

repos.description: Unified embedded-hal driver traits for common environmental sensors
repos.readme_text:
# hal-sensors

A trait layer for environmental sensors (temperature, humidity, pressure, VOC) so application code stops depending on a specific part number.

```rust
let mut sensor: Box<dyn EnvironmentalSensor> = Box::new(BME280::new(i2c));
let reading = sensor.read()?;
```

Supports `no-std`. Currently covers 11 sensors. Contributions for new parts welcome.

repos.description: Diff tokenizers across model versions to catch silent tokenization regressions
repos.readme_text:
# tokenizer-diff

When a provider ships a new tokenizer revision, the model version stays the same and your prompts silently re-tokenize. This tool shows you exactly which strings changed.

```bash
tokenizer-diff --model-a gpt-4o-2024-11 --model-b gpt-4o-2025-02 --corpus prompts.txt
```

Small utility, one job.
